31.s: He describes a tiny gunman holding up the Mummers Club on 33rd Street, and seeing the robbers partying at Small's, saying they were sending money to Sing Sing.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: Another place I used to -- down to Mummer's Club, down on 33rd Street and one night, it was on a Saturday night and I was there and the place started fillingup and all these men come in and I said -- I don't know who it was, but I said so and so shouldn't let all these men in here, and I hadn't no…

31.t: Loft nightclub, Mummers Club, Cat's Meow and Chapman night
31.s: Whaley retells playing the loft club with singer Mary Strange, Jack Legs Diamond, a holdup, the Cat's Meow and the Prisoner's Song.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Right. I started playing around these clubs, see, to get a job, and we went down on the -- on Broadway there, 1800 block, in there, between 56th and 57th Street. Or 55th and 56th Street, there's a big building there, and it was a loft, see, and they had a nightclub up there and I got a job there,…

31.t: Band at a Broadway loft nightclub where Jack Legs Diamond sat
31.s: Whaley led a band for a 56th Street loft club where entertainers split tips, and quit after white girls replaced them and he learned a customer was gangster Jack Legs Diamond.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: Broadway. They had lofts there and these guys, I don't know who they were but anyway, they opened it up as a nightclub and I used to have the band there, see, and they used to have colored entertainers and a colored entertainer, if they get a dollar, they give me 50 cents, see.

31.t: Leading his own bands in Harlem, the Chapman execution night and Casper's
31.s: Barred from the Clef Club, Whaley builds his own band, plays a Harlem Italian place on gangster Gerald Chapman's execution night, and recalls Small's opening and Casper's.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: He had all the gigs, like the Clef Club. If you get in the Clef Club, you are already made, but they didn't want no outsiders in there. They wouldn't let me in there, so finally I got the break with Lucky and I started doing a whole lot of things then. I got myself a band and used to play over in…

31.t: Unpaid at the gangster-run Cat's Meow
31.s: At the Cat's Meow in Brooklyn the owner owed him a week's pay, hit him in the office, and Whaley told the band not to play.
31.ch: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
31.q: I remember over at the Cat's Meow in Brooklyn, the gangsters run that place and they had a show, chorus girls and everything and the man owed me money for a week and he said he's going to give to me when I open up but he didn't give it to me so I wouldn't play there, no, you got to give us some…

26.s: Greer describes Wilkins as stubborn and says he was shot before the Cotton Club years.
26.q: A very unassuming man, you know. Very quiet-spoken. But when he said something, he meant it. He was high with the syndicate, you know. And Baron Wilkins, he was stubborn. That's how he got killed, he was very stubborn. If he didn't think something was right he'd just go ahead and forgot it.

26.t: Settling bets for racketeers at Lindy's
26.s: Gangsters ask Greer to settle bets across from Lindy's.
26.q: They like that, you see. They like me, because if I thought someone was right I'd come on. I didn't know the word "back". Because a lot of the times I'd be coming -- standing on Broadway and 49th Street and across the street was Lindsey's (Lindy's) a very famous -- that was the hangout for all the…

26.t: Casper Holstein, Dutch Schultz and Owney Madden
26.s: Greer names who controlled the numbers and says Owney Madden was top.
26.q: Casper Hostein, I know him, the number man. Yeah, he was one of the few colored guys -- he was a numbers back-up. They kidnapped him, sure. But they turned him loose because he was closely associated. 'Cause they put the word out, "turn him loose." Whenever the Syndicate says, "that's my man," that…

26.t: Gangsters and the Revenue men at the Kentucky Club
26.s: Gangsters like Legs Diamond and Luciano frequent the club; boss Leo Bernstein relies on Greer to vet who can drink.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: You'd hear a colored boy named Slim upstairs and that's when the Revenue men were breaking down the doors, you know, because we was selling whiskey. We sold everybody, but couldn't nobody get to drink in my club unless

1.t: Steele and the Barron Wilkins and Jack Legs Diamond killings
1.s: Steele worked at Barron Wilkins's club when Charleston killed Wilkins, and had to flee to Albany after he witnessed a gangland shooting.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Who was who. He was working in Barron Wilkins' joint as a waiter when Charleston killed Barron Wilkins. Barron Wilkins had the big nightclub where Ethel Waters and them went, on 135th Street. And his brother had Wilkins' on the other side of the street, that was one of the greatest nightclubs in…

1.s: Danny describes the Italian and Spanish racketeers' floating dice games in rented apartments and the high stakes he played music beside.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: That's Italian racketeers, Spanish racketeers, they have floating dice games. They gamble like crazy. They don't stay in one spot. They'll rent an apartment like on the fourth or fifth or sixth floor, and they stake it out, and... The real estate, they've got a deal with the guy. And they come up…

1.t: The second dice-game job: police, gate and spaghetti
1.s: Bill took Danny to another job, waiting until exactly the right minute to enter, where the mobsters loved Bill and fed them.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: Then he said, "I've got another one." And we go to another place. And we parked in front of a house. And we parked in front of a house, and there is an apartment in another building, another (?). And we wait. I said, "Man, I'm scared up in this dark neighborhood. Man, the (?) people looking at some…

97.t: Harry Ross's band and the Connie's Inn gig
97.s: Scott joins the Connie's Inn band and learns it has been rented to Dutch Schultz.
97.q: Well, he was going to open up at -- because he was a member of the Amsterdam, and he caught up down at the Amsterdam. I went there one night just to look around. I was still playing the Lafayette. He says, (unintelligible). Connie Simms was right by the Lafayette, but it was downstairs.

97.t: Small's Paradise and Charlie Johnson's band
97.s: Ed Small's club, a run-in with a gangster over a showgirl, and Charlie Johnson.
97.q: And I associated and I met plenty of people, and there was Ed Small. He was boss of -- he owned Small's Paradise. Charlie Johnson was in there, had the band for years. Charlie and I became very good friends. I used to go in there, and one time there was a showgirl that I took up there once, and…

97.t: Duplicate: Connie's Inn and Dutch Schultz
97.q: went there and never went in there. Colored people didn't go in there, strictly white people. And I said, where you going, Connie's Inn? He say, yeah. He says, I want you to rehease with us. He named a place and he had a rehearsal band and all like that.

89.t: Leroy's cabaret and the shootout behind the piano
89.s: He worked at Leroy's at 135th and Fifth, a rough black cabaret with Jenkins Orphanage men in the band, where the band hid behind the piano during shooting.
89.q: I would say 50. About 50 years were my headquarters there. You know, back and forth to Europe or Africa, but New York was home.

89.t: Snowden's band at the Hot Feet Club and Boston Blackie
89.s: He played in Elmer Snowden's eight-piece band at a Village gangster club, with entertainers and the original Boston Blackie pasting bills on waiters.
89.q: passed on last year too, one of the greats. I've mentioned his name already in connection with Duke Ellington. He had the band that brought Duke Ellington to New York. I'm referring to Elmer Snowden again. This time I'd like to tell of my experience with Snowden when he had the band at the famous…

30.t: The gangster who wanted 'Singing in the Rain' at the Cotton Club
30.s: A newly released gangster asked Duke for 'Singing in the Rain', Duke put him off, and after the manager Herman Stark explained who the man was the band played it for an hour.
30.q: I got to tell you this good one about Duke. You know, Duke, he's contrary at times, you know, like people would come in and ask him to play a tune and he'll give you that grin, "Yeah. Okay, yeah." So this is at the Cotton Club and this gangster had did time for one of the big bosses there.

30.t: The gangster as Duke's bodyguard and rival mobs
30.s: The gangster became Duke's bodyguard with a machine gun and bulletproof glass because of rival factions of Owney Madden and Capone; Willard mentions a Legs Diamond tip.
30.q: all these big guys, you know, like, Rudy Vallee when he was in his prime and all that, this guy was Duke's bodyguard. He'd go get Duke from the theater with his machine gun between his legs, and they had a bulletproof glass.

251.t: Keeping order and the clientele at the Keyhole
251.s: Albert hired peace officers to prevent fights and his customers were San Antonio's respectable people.
251.q: Mm-hm. Mm-hm. And then to by being the first to get to neighboring this arrangement, I want it to be perfect because I was threatened to have it closed if anything would happen in between the races, which never would come across people's mind. They were there for entertainment. I had the best…

430.t: Saratoga Club and Casper Holstein as boss
430.s: Barbarin describes the basement club on Lenox Avenue and Holstein as a kind employer who paid on Mondays, and the story of his kidnapping.
430.q: All this place happened to be down in the basement, you know? It was down in the basement. I had a full show there. It was a good show. Casper Holstein, which was the proprietor, he was a very nice man. You didn't have to worry about your money. I mean, whether he did business or not, he always had…

946.t: Smoky clubs, low pay and the mob
946.s: Davern loved smoky clubs; Domber says mobsters owned clubs and hired jazz musicians.
946.q: They always worked the thirty dollar gigs, or at that time the thirty-five dollar gigs in places, you know, in the smoky bars. But they had a certain joy of doing it. Kenny Davern used to tell me that he loved the smoke, he loved the atmosphere of the clubs and the bars, you know, thick with smoke…

85.t: Shot-up spaghetti joint in Brooklyn and gangsters in the music business
85.s: A mob shooting at a Brooklyn club, and what Carter knew of mobsters at Connie's Inn and the Cotton Club.
85.q: Not by name at the moment. One thing stands out in my mind. I know that we played in what we called a spaghetti joint in Brooklyn, and what we think were some mobsters came in one night and kind of shot up the place. I think I got out of there, but Willy found or sought refuge in the gents’ room…

101.t: Gangsters, Billy Eckstine and the Jo Jones story
101.s: Gangsters ran the clubs; the story of Jo Jones brought from Kansas City to the Plantation.
101.q: It could possibly be. I never heard that before. I’m born and raised in St. Louis, but I never heard it. Not to say that it couldn’t be true, but . . . possibly it’s true.

67.t: Gangsters at the Cotton Club and a show at Sing Sing
67.s: Gangsters were friendly, well-dressed bosses who ran the Cotton Club; Cab's whole show once played Sing Sing for an imprisoned mobster.
67.q: but nice, friendly, but you could tell they were the boss, you know, a lot of them came in the Cotton Club, when I was with Cab, I knew a lot of them, they came over. We went to Sing Sing and played a little benefit, a whole Cotton Club show for one of the mobsters up there, he was in there.

9.t: Getting the Nest Club job and playing for gangsters
9.s: A phone call to the Bandbox sent him to the Nest, where drummer-leader George Howe and pianist Luis Russell hired him, and gangsters threw money after 3 a.m.
9.q: : At that time, I'm waiting for Chick to go to work, and I had just finished with (?)'s band. Now, here I'm standing in the Rhythm Club or the Bandbox, whatever you call it, and a phone call comes in for "Holmes, the saxophone player, don't forget to bring your horn around to the Nest Club." Well,…

0.t: Playing in the Village for gangsters
0.s: He worked Greenwich Village bands where gangsters ran the clubs.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s

76.t: The New Deal Club on the West Side
76.s: Zutty describes the New Deal Club, a rough West Side joint run by Charlie with gangsters' sons, where Marge once filled in on piano with her long fingernails.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Oh the New Deal, that was just a little joint over on the West Side. They had a lot of gangsters sons who would come in. And I even had Marge come over one night to play the piano for me.

7.t: The gangsters wreck a rival Harlem club
7.s: A would-be rival club on 125th Street that ignored the Cotton Club's warning is vandalized overnight, so the show never opens.
7.ch: Cotton Club and radio fame with Cab
7.q: See, the Cotton Club wanted to move downtown, but for some reason or another they couldn't move down there. So eventually, they worked out a deal... We found out... See, they did it right. Because we was foolin' around with another guy, with some clubs in New York. And they told this guy "Don't…

112.t: The killing of Baron Wilkins by Yellow Charleston
112.s: He says Italian gangsters used a deprived addict, Yellow Charleston, to shoot Baron, and Harlem sportsmen hunted him.
112.q: thing. They got hold of a black man that was a dope fiend. Yellow Charleston. They got ahold of Yellow Charleston and they shut him off, isolated him from all dope. Until he was like this. They told him, "Look, if you want to get dope and all the dope you want, you've got to shoot Old Man Baron."…
